title: Chapter 23: Celia Opens the Second Drawer
content: The tape is the good tape and it still will not hold in this wind.

Wren is up the ladder at the boat shed with the roll in her teeth when the car comes down the lane. It is small and silver and clean and it takes the ruts badly, and it stops where the gravel ends and does not come any further, which tells her who it is before the door opens.
Celia Reeve gets out in a cream coat and town shoes and a scarf tied like a catalogue, and stands in the cold with a tin of biscuits from the gas station held in both hands.
"Is this a bad time?"
"It is a time."
"I brought these." She holds out the tin. "You do not come to a house empty-handed. That is the whole of what I know about houses."
Wren comes down the ladder and takes the tin and says, "The stove is on."

The kitchen is the kitchen. His chair. The two dictionaries. The lamp with the crack in the shade. Four sheets of the log taped to the inside of the window, because the outside ones keep going, and a fifth sheet on the table with the corners curled from being carried in a coat.
Celia stands in the middle of the floor and does not sit.
"Sit," Wren says. "Not that one."
Celia sits in the other one, on the edge, the way a person sits in a waiting room where the receptionist has already been rude to somebody else.

The kettle is a dented thing that takes four minutes. Wren puts tea in two cups without asking, because asking is a conversation and she does not want one yet, and sets one down in front of Celia and one on the other side of the table, and sits down.

Celia puts something on the table between them. It is a key. Small, brass, with a paper tag on a string, and on the tag, in a hand Wren has seen on ninety thousand dollars and nine clauses, two words: second drawer.
"Before I tell you what I found," Celia says, "you need to know what I did."
"I know what you did. You took a key out of your mother's house."
"I have had a copy of that key since I was fourteen."
Wren looks at her.

"I was fourteen," Celia says, "and there was a drawer in my mother's study with a lock on it, and a lock is a lock. I did not even want what was in it. I wanted the drawer to be open because she had closed it."
"What is in it?"

"Paper." Celia wraps both hands around the cup. "That is the thing nobody understands about my mother. Everybody thinks she is hiding something. She is not hiding. She is keeping. There are forty-one folders in the second drawer, in order, oldest at the front, each one a copy of a file the county has, with a cover sheet in her hand. She does not grieve, Miss Aubrey. She indexes."
Wren takes the key off the table and turns it over. It is warm from Celia's hand and it has been cut twice, once by a locksmith and once badly.
"There is one at the back with nothing in it," Celia says. "An empty folder. The tab says Kessler in pencil. She made it before the county did."
The stove ticks. Out on the river a piece of ice goes down the piling with a sound like a spoon in a drawer.
"When did you open it?" Wren says.

"Nineteen. I opened it once at nineteen and I closed it and I did not go back." Celia's eyes come up. "I am not proud of the six years. I want that in the record, whatever the record is. Six years of knowing there was a drawer and letting it be a drawer."
"Why now?"

"Because of your sheets." Celia says it without ornament. "I stood in front of the diner on Monday with everybody else and read a column from 1953 and thought, my uncle is not on this. He is not on this because he did not cross. He went in at the gate, and the gate is not the ferry, and so he is not on the paper and he is not in the ground under his own name."
Wren says nothing.

"I went to the cemetery when I was fourteen," Celia says. "There is a stone in the Reeve plot with a name I had never heard in my life. Hugh. Nineteen fifty-seven to nineteen ninety-eight. Nobody in that house has said the name Hugh in twenty years. I asked my mother who he was and she said, my brother, and then she asked me to pass the salt."
"He worked at the gate."

"He ran the night shift at the gate. He had done it since eighty-nine. He was forty-one and he had a boat and a bad knee and a dog, and on the fourth of July in ninety-eight the town had fireworks at the fairground, and at twenty past nine the gate let go."
Wren sets the cup down.
"The fireworks," she says.

"Every dog in the county was screaming. My mother says the siren ran. She says it ran and nobody could hear it, which is a different sentence than the siren did not run, and she has had twenty-eight years to decide which one she says, and she has never once said the same one twice."
Celia's hands are steady now. That is the worst part. She has rehearsed this in a car.

"He was on the water," she says. "Below the gate, in the aluminum boat, taking a sample off the trash rack, because the intake had been clogging all summer and he did not want to wake a man at ten at night to hold a torch for him. That is what the report says. One man in a boat, after dark, on a release night."
"Whose decision was that?"

"His. And hers, for staffing the shift with one man." Celia's mouth does something and stops. "If the county had called it a gate death there would have been an inquiry. An inquiry reads the release log. The release log says the gate ran at twenty past nine at night, which the schedule did not allow then either, and it says there was one man on the water, and it says the Authority sent him."
Wren looks at the key in her hand.
"So she made it a boating accident."

"She made it a man in a boat who hit something in the dark." Celia reaches into her coat and brings out a large envelope, soft at the corners, the flap held with string. "Which is almost true. That is the thing I cannot get past. It is almost true. He was in a boat, it was dark, he hit something. Every word of it is a word. It is the order of the words that kills him twice."
She puts the envelope on the table and does not push it across.

"I am not doing this for you," she says. "I want to be clear, because you are the kind of person who will decide I am kind and then be disappointed. I am not on your side. I am not on anybody's side. I am on the side of the thing that happened."
"All right."
"You are supposed to argue with me. People argue with me. They say, Celia, your mother loves you, and then I have to sit there with my face."
"Does she love you?"

"Yes." Celia says it flatly. "That is not the question. The question is what she would spend. She spent her brother. She spent him in one afternoon and she has kept the receipt in a drawer for twenty-eight years. And I am the daughter of the woman who signs the permits, and I am engaged to the engineer who signed the survey, and I have understood for some time that I am a thing she maintains."
The wind takes the corner of the sheet on the table and lifts it and sets it down.
"You are marrying the engineer," Wren says.

"In April. If there is an April." Celia looks at the window. "He is not sleeping. He has been sleeping at the office, on a cot in the survey room, under a blanket that belongs to the county." She turns her cup a quarter turn, and it is such an exact copy of her mother that Wren has to look away. "He thinks I do not know about the transfer. It has been in a tray since October."
"Then it is real."

"It has been real since October. That is what a tray is for." Celia's voice stays level. "He has been walking the levee at night with a clipboard. My mother calls it diligence. I call it a man looking for a place to put his hands."
Wren does not answer that, because there is no answer that is not a door.
"Open it," Celia says. "Or I will. But I would rather you did. It should be opened by somebody who has been in the water."
Wren pulls the string. The envelope has been opened and closed so many times that the flap is furred.
Inside is one folder, thin, the county's buff, with a number in the corner and a name typed on a strip of paper and glued down, the way they did it before the machines: REEVE, HUGH A.
She opens it on the table between the cups.
The top sheet is a Report of Death, Unwitnessed. Two pages, typed, with a box for cause and a box for manner and a third box that says remarks.
Cause: struck by a submerged object.
Manner: boating accident.
Place: Sable River, Mile 12, below Kettler Gate.
Date of loss: 4 July 1998.
Below that, in the remarks box, in a hand she has seen on a check and on nine clauses and on a paper tag: no autopsy. family request. no inquiry. O. Reeve.
"That is not the county's hand," Wren says.
"No."
"That is your mother's hand on a county form."

"She was a district engineer in ninety-eight. She was not the director. She was the person who drove to the courthouse at eight on the Monday morning and stood at the window until it was done." Celia's voice has gone quiet. "The clerk who took it is on the stamp."
Wren turns the page.

The stamp is at the bottom, in violet, gone grey at the edges, the way county stamps go: RECEIVED, TOWN CLERK, 6 JUL 1998, and under it a box with initials and a name, because in 1998 the town still put the clerk's name in the box instead of a number.
H. DRANE, CLERK.
The radiator knocks. Wren puts a finger on the stamp and leaves it there.
"He was thirty-three," she says. "In 1998. Hollis Drane was thirty-three years old and he was at that window on the Monday morning."
Celia leans in to look.
"Who is Drane?"
Wren closes the folder.
"He is the man who has my grandfather in his drawer," she says. "He stamped this in July of ninety-eight and went home to his dinner, and on Saturday he is going to have to say so out loud."
Celia stands and winds her scarf twice.
"I will need it back by Friday morning. I am filing it myself, as an exhibit, before the hearing, and I am not going to hand it to a clerk and stand there while she reads it."
"All right."
At the door she stops with her hand on the frame and does not turn around.
"You should know that I am not going to testify. A daughter who testifies is a weather event. A daughter who files is a fact."
She goes out to the car in her town shoes and the gravel is loud under them all the way to the road.

Wren puts the key down and sets the folder on top of the five sheets and the two dictionaries and the lamp with the crack in the shade. Outside, the river goes by half a foot above where it was at noon, brown and patient. The paper tag on the key says second drawer, in a hand that signs things.
highlight: Celia Reeve brings Wren the key tagged second drawer and the 1998 file her mother buried.
